Feature cards Nine card layouts, in light and dark

Relay answers your customers, and hands the hard ones to your team.

Relay is an assistant for online shops. It answers customer emails, chats and calls from your help center and order data, and passes the hard cases to a person.

One assistant for the whole inbox. It answers, acts and asks for help when it should.

01 / 2x2 grid

Answers from your help center

Relay reads your help articles and past replies, and shows where each answer came from.

Works inside your helpdesk

It picks up tickets in Zendesk, replies and updates the status, like a person on your team.

Relay6 open ticketsRunning

Hands off when it should

Refunds over your limit or an upset customer go straight to a person, with the full history.

Follows your rules

Choose what Relay may do on its own, from refunds to order changes.

Set up in an afternoon. Connect what you already wrote and choose how it looks.

<!doctype html>
<html lang="en"><head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Object render</title>
<style>body{margin:0;background:#888}canvas{display:block}</style></head>
<body>
<canvas id="c" width="300" height="340"></canvas>
<script>
/* A stoneware mug modelled and lit in code (signed distance fields, one fragment shader), rendered once with
   alpha and handed to shoot.mjs make as a PNG: the demo cut-out for the object scenes. Colours: ?body=e8e1d4&glaze=6f7f7a */
window.addEventListener('error', e => { window.__err = e.message; });
try {
const q = new URLSearchParams(location.search);
const hexv = (s, d) => { const h = (s || d).replace('#', ''); return [0, 2, 4].map(i => parseInt(h.slice(i, i + 2), 16) / 255); };
const body = hexv(q.get('body'), 'e8e1d4'), glaze = hexv(q.get('glaze'), '5f6e6a');
const cv = document.getElementById('c');
const g = cv.getContext('webgl', { alpha: true, premultipliedAlpha: false, preserveDrawingBuffer: true, antialias: false });
const V = 'attribute vec2 a_p;varying vec2 v_uv;void main(){v_uv=a_p*0.5+0.5;gl_Position=vec4(a_p,0.0,1.0);}';
const F = `
precision highp float;
varying vec2 v_uv;
uniform vec2 u_res; uniform vec3 u_body; uniform vec3 u_glaze;
float sdCyl(vec3 p, float h, float r){ vec2 d = abs(vec2(length(p.xz), p.y)) - vec2(r, h); return min(max(d.x, d.y), 0.0) + length(max(d, 0.0)); }
float sdTor(vec3 p, vec2 t){ vec2 d = vec2(length(p.xy) - t.x, p.z); return length(d) - t.y; }
vec2 map(vec3 p){
  // body: a slightly tapered cup, hollow, with a lip
  float taper = 1.0 + 0.06 * (p.y + 0.55) ;
  vec3 pb = vec3(p.x / taper, p.y, p.z / taper);
  float outer = sdCyl(pb, 0.62, 0.42) - 0.03;
  float inner = sdCyl(pb - vec3(0.0, 0.14, 0.0), 0.62, 0.36);
  float cup = max(outer, -inner);
  // handle: a torus segment on +x, slightly squashed
  vec3 ph = p - vec3(0.46, 0.0, 0.0);
  float handle = sdTor(vec3(ph.x * 1.1, ph.y * 0.78, ph.z), vec2(0.30, 0.058));
  float cutH = -(ph.x + 0.02);  // keep only the outer half of the ring
  handle = max(handle, cutH);
  float d = min(cup, handle);
  // material id: 1 outer glaze band near the foot, 0 body
  float id = (p.y < -0.30 && cup < handle) ? 1.0 : 0.0;
  // inside of the cup is glazed too
  if (cup < handle && inner < 0.02 && p.y > -0.44) id = 1.0;
  return vec2(d, id);
}
vec3 nrm(vec3 p){ vec2 e = vec2(0.0015, 0.0); return normalize(vec3(map(p + e.xyy).x - map(p - e.xyy).x, map(p + e.yxy).x - map(p - e.yxy).x, map(p + e.yyx).x - map(p - e.yyx).x)); }
float ao(vec3 p, vec3 n){ float o = 0.0, s = 1.0; for (int i = 1; i <= 5; i++){ float h = 0.03 * float(i); float d = map(p + n * h).x; o += (h - d) * s; s *= 0.6; } return clamp(1.0 - 2.2 * o, 0.0, 1.0); }
float shadow(vec3 ro, vec3 rd){ float r = 1.0, t = 0.02; for (int i = 0; i < 48; i++){ float h = map(ro + rd * t).x; r = min(r, 12.0 * h / t); t += clamp(h, 0.01, 0.08); if (h < 0.0005 || t > 3.0) break; } return clamp(r, 0.0, 1.0); }
void main(){
  vec2 uv = (gl_FragCoord.xy - 0.5 * u_res) / u_res.y;
  vec3 ro = vec3(0.0, 0.35, 3.1);
  vec3 ta = vec3(0.0, -0.02, 0.0);
  vec3 fw = normalize(ta - ro), rt = normalize(cross(fw, vec3(0.0, 1.0, 0.0))), up = cross(rt, fw);
  vec3 rd = normalize(uv.x * rt + uv.y * up + 1.9 * fw);
  // turn the mug a little so the handle shows
  float a = 0.62; mat3 R = mat3(cos(a), 0.0, sin(a), 0.0, 1.0, 0.0, -sin(a), 0.0, cos(a));
  float t = 0.0; vec2 h = vec2(0.0); bool hit = false;
  for (int i = 0; i < 140; i++){ vec3 p = R * (ro + rd * t); h = map(p); if (h.x < 0.0008){ hit = true; break; } t += h.x * 0.9; if (t > 7.0) break; }
  if (!hit){ gl_FragColor = vec4(0.0); return; }
  vec3 p = R * (ro + rd * t); vec3 n = nrm(p);
  vec3 L1 = normalize(vec3(-0.55, 0.9, 0.5)), L2 = normalize(vec3(0.7, 0.25, -0.3));
  float d1 = max(dot(n, L1), 0.0), d2 = max(dot(n, L2), 0.0);
  float sh = shadow(p + n * 0.004, L1);
  float occ = ao(p, n);
  vec3 base = mix(u_body, u_glaze, h.y);
  vec3 col = base * (0.30 * occ + 0.72 * d1 * sh + 0.22 * d2) ;
  // soft sheen for the glaze
  vec3 vdir = normalize(-rd * R);
  vec3 hv = normalize(L1 + (R * vdir));
  float spec = pow(max(dot(n, hv), 0.0), mix(18.0, 60.0, h.y)) * mix(0.08, 0.35, h.y) * sh;
  col += spec;
  col = pow(col, vec3(0.95));
  gl_FragColor = vec4(col, 1.0);
}`;
const sh = (t, s) => { const o = g.createShader(t); g.shaderSource(o, s); g.compileShader(o); if (!g.getShaderParameter(o, g.COMPILE_STATUS)) throw new Error(g.getShaderInfoLog(o)); return o; };
const prog = g.createProgram(); g.attachShader(prog, sh(g.VERTEX_SHADER, V)); g.attachShader(prog, sh(g.FRAGMENT_SHADER, F)); g.linkProgram(prog);
if (!g.getProgramParameter(prog, g.LINK_STATUS)) throw new Error(g.getProgramInfoLog(prog));
g.useProgram(prog);
const b = g.createBuffer(); g.bindBuffer(g.ARRAY_BUFFER, b); g.bufferData(g.ARRAY_BUFFER, new Float32Array([-1, -1, 3, -1, -1, 3]), g.STATIC_DRAW);
const l = g.getAttribLocation(prog, 'a_p'); g.enableVertexAttribArray(l); g.vertexAttribPointer(l, 2, g.FLOAT, false, 0, 0);
g.viewport(0, 0, cv.width, cv.height);
g.uniform2f(g.getUniformLocation(prog, 'u_res'), cv.width, cv.height);
g.uniform3f(g.getUniformLocation(prog, 'u_body'), ...body);
g.uniform3f(g.getUniformLocation(prog, 'u_glaze'), ...glaze);
g.clearColor(0, 0, 0, 0); g.clear(g.COLOR_BUFFER_BIT);
g.drawArrays(g.TRIANGLES, 0, 3);
g.finish();
// trim: find the opaque bounds and crop to them with a small margin, so the PNG's bottom row is the foot
const px = new Uint8Array(cv.width * cv.height * 4); g.readPixels(0, 0, cv.width, cv.height, g.RGBA, g.UNSIGNED_BYTE, px);
let x0 = cv.width, x1 = 0, y0 = cv.height, y1 = 0;
for (let y = 0; y < cv.height; y++) for (let x = 0; x < cv.width; x++) if (px[(y * cv.width + x) * 4 + 3] > 8) { x0 = Math.min(x0, x); x1 = Math.max(x1, x); y0 = Math.min(y0, y); y1 = Math.max(y1, y); }
const out = document.createElement('canvas'); const m = 6;
out.width = x1 - x0 + 1 + 2 * m; out.height = y1 - y0 + 1 + 2 * m;
const ctx = out.getContext('2d');
const img = ctx.createImageData(out.width, out.height);
for (let y = 0; y < out.height; y++) for (let x = 0; x < out.width; x++) {
  const sx = x0 - m + x, sy = (cv.height - 1) - (y0 - m + y); // flip: GL rows start at the bottom
  const o = (y * out.width + x) * 4;
  if (sx < 0 || sy < 0 || sx >= cv.width || sy >= cv.height) continue;
  const s = (sy * cv.width + sx) * 4;
  img.data[o] = px[s]; img.data[o + 1] = px[s + 1]; img.data[o + 2] = px[s + 2]; img.data[o + 3] = px[s + 3];
}
ctx.putImageData(img, 0, 0);
window.__out = out.toDataURL('image/png');
document.body.appendChild(out);
} catch (e) { window.__err = String(e && e.message || e); }
</script>
</body></html>

objects/index.html:
Objects
Print objects Photo prints Scenes
Paper

Objects for one strong moment a page.

Products drawn in code, photographs printed by a shader, and scenes that answer the pointer. A photograph leads where there is one. An object leads where there is none.

  • Print objects 05
  • Photo prints 03
  • Scenes 05

01 Print object

Cup and saucer

A porcelain cup of coffee on its saucer, the glaze in your accent. Click it to stir.

Leads
A tableware maker with no photographs
As a print
A software card about a morning
GPU
High while it turns, one frame at rest

Morning digest

One email at 8:00 with everything that changed overnight.

02 Print object

Bicycle wheel

A road wheel with a tan-wall tyre, an alloy rim and 24 spokes, the hub in your accent. Click it to spin it up.

Leads
A maker of wheels or hubs, never a whole bike
As a print
A card about speed or a mechanism
GPU
High while it turns, one frame at rest

Background sync

Runs every five minutes, whether the app is open or not.

03 Print object

Desk lamp

A balanced-arm desk lamp on chrome springs, the base and shade enamelled in your accent. Click it to switch it on.

Leads
A lighting maker with no photographs
As a print
A card about focus or working late
GPU
High while it moves, one frame at rest

Focus mode

Alerts wait until you switch it off.

04 Print object

Desk globe

A desk globe with the real coastlines, a brass meridian and a walnut stand. Its sea takes a blue or teal accent. Click it to spin.

Leads
A maker of globes or maps
As a print
A card about regions or shipping
GPU
High while it turns, one frame at rest

14 regions

Pick where your data lives. Move it later in two clicks.

05 Print object

Playing cards

A stack of playing cards, the ace of diamonds face up and the backs in your accent. Click to fan them out.

Leads
A maker of card or board games
As a print
A games card about a hand or a deal
GPU
High while it moves, one frame at rest

Fair draws

Every shuffle is logged, so any player can check a deal.

06 Photo print

Halftone photograph

One photograph in one ink: round dots on a 45° screen, clean paper in the light. Point at it and a loupe shows its colour.

Use
One photograph band on a design or software page
Never
A hero photograph, a cafe, a guesthouse
GPU
Low, one context, still at rest

Screens for print

Send any photograph to press as a one-ink halftone.

07 Photo print

Engraved photograph

Diagonal lines that swell in the shadows and bend over the forms, over a light wash of the photograph's colour. Point at it and the lines part.

Use
A tile whose subject is the photograph
Never
A hero photograph, a cafe, a guesthouse
GPU
Low, one context, still at rest

Line art from a photo

Turn a product shot into a plate for packaging.

08 Photo print

Dithered photograph

A three-colour grain from the photograph's deepest and most colourful tones. Point at it and the photograph develops through the grain.

Use
A games or AI page's one photograph
Never
A hero photograph, a cafe, a guesthouse
GPU
Low, one context, still at rest

Three colours, any picture

A grain that keeps a photograph readable in two inks and the paper.

09 Scene

Split reveal

One photograph, half of it printed as a halftone screen. The line follows the pointer; on a phone it follows a drag.

Use
A photo or design app, a device, a game's key art
Never
A place, a service, a product page
GPU
Low, drawn only while the line moves

Before and after

Drag the line to compare the print with the original.

10 Scene

Dither sequence

Two to six photographs that belong together, dithered and cut one to the next like a slow film. Move across it to pick a frame.

Use
A device from several sides, a game's scenes
Never
A random or mood set of pictures
GPU
Low, drawn only during a cut

Every version kept

Step back through earlier versions of a picture.

11 Scene

Dot object

An object cut out of its photograph and set in dots that keep its tones. Under the pointer the dots take its real colour.

Use
A thing shot on a plain ground, or a cut-out
Never
A busy or sunlit background
GPU
Low, one draw call while the loupe moves

Cut-outs in one click

The ground is read from the border and left out.

12 Scene

Exploded layers

One photograph as four printed sheets in perspective. Hover and they open apart, each named in the product's own words.

Use
Software that works in layers: imaging, maps
Never
Sheets named after the effects
GPU
Low, drawn only while it opens

Edits you can undo

Turn any layer off later without touching the rest.

13 Scene

Product turntable

A camera, a chair, a speaker or a cup, stepping round on a studio turntable. Move across it to turn it yourself.

Use
A kind of thing the software handles
Never
The client's own product
GPU
Low, drawn only while it steps

See it from every side

Check each piece from all angles before you rent it.

objects/product-render/README.md:
# Product render (`assets/objects/product-render`) A studio render of **any physical product**, composed from a short JSON spec: a list of parts with sizes and positions in the product's own units. `build.js` turns the spec into a model and `_print-core/print3d.js` renders it: real materials (painted metal, alloy, chrome, rubber, wood, fabric, leather, plastic, a light), soft studio light with soft shadows, a softbox in glossy parts, a floor shadow, the page's accent on the parts that ask for it. It sways slowly as a turntable, or holds still; a lamp switches on and off on a click; a robot's joints move. Use it when the **brief asks for 3D or a render** (a configurator, a product that exists only as a model): the render is the product's picture, in the hero and the statement. A product without photographs and without that ask is shown in photographs, its own or stand-ins (`references/photos.md`). Never for a product that has photographs, never on a place page, never captioned, never a product of another kind. One product render a page. ## Mount: the product at anchor scale ```html
``` The frame is the picture: the product's own bounds fill a share of it (the tighter way, width or height) and it stands on the page's ground with its floor shadow, transparent round it: **no panel, no grey box**. Give the frame its size (a hero column as tall as the screen, a full-width stage, a tile); the product fills it. | attribute | | |---|---| | `data-product-place` | `hero` 0.88, `stage` 0.86, `tile` 0.84, `card` 0.9 of the frame (`legacy`: the old turntable right of the words) | | `data-product-view` | `three-quarter` (default), then only the views the spec lists in `supports` (`side`, `front`, `top`, a close-up of its own such as `detail-saddle`); `product.views` lists them; any other (the bike's `top`) throws and the frame carries `data-product-error`; or `detail:` | | `data-product-scene` | a scene of the spec: the product loaded or in use (`loaded`, `desk`, `work`) | | `data-product-color` | a colourway id of the spec (`spec.colors`); default its first | | `data-product-mode` | `auto` (default): the still make-posters made, else the turn, else one frame rendered here; `image`, `still`, `live` force one | | `data-product-fill` | 0.3-1.2, over the place's share | | `data-product-params` | `{"turn":1}` asks for the live turn; `{"x":0.1,"y":-0.05}` moves it; `{"step":0}` a lamp off | | `data-product-palette` | `{ bg, surface, ink, accent }`; else the page's tokens `--bg`, `--ink`, `--accent` | **Each section a different view.** A product page shows the product big, whole in three sections at most, and never the same view twice: the widest view in the hero (a bike's `side`; a lamp's or an arm's `three-quarter`), another angle by the specs, a close-up on the part a section talks about, the loaded scene where the copy promises what it carries. Every promise in a headline is shown in a picture (a child seat with its belts, the crates, a lamp's light on the desk). **A close-up** (`detail-*`, `detail:`) frames the named parts and centres them on the frame (their box, `focus` in the manifest, fills the place's share); the rest of the product runs off the frame's edges (the frame clips it), never a hard cut inside it. So that holds in a wide tile too, a close-up's shot is made wide enough (`cover`, default 2: a frame up to twice as wide as tall, 1 : 1.25 tall) with the product running on past the parts as far as it goes, and its still is cropped evenly round the parts' centre, never to the product's own box. **Colour from an order card.** A swatch drives the frames it names, no script needed: ```html ``` On click (a button: `aria-pressed` is kept, one pressed per group) or change (an input), the named frames (default: every frame whose spec has that colourway) set `data-product-color` and swap to that colour's still. Setting `data-product-color`, `-view` or `-scene` on a mounted frame does the same, and so does an event: `el.dispatchEvent(new CustomEvent('product:set', { detail: { color: 'red', view: 'side' } }))`, or on `document` with `detail.target` a selector. **What a frame tells** (for checkers and tests): `data-product-mode`, `data-product-state` (`image` | `still` | `live` | `poster`), `data-product-view`, `data-product-color-shown`; the picture is `img.product-render__img`; `window.__tpProduct` = `{ stills, images, live, freed }`. In `image` mode the page holds no canvas and no WebGL context; a `still` renders once, keeps an ``, frees its context and removes its canvases; only `live` keeps a context (and counts in `window.__tpGl`). A product page uses the stills (the default once make-posters has run). A `still` is measured (its opaque pixels, and a close-up's parts) and placed by the same layout as a poster still, so it fills its place's share exactly (tile .84) and is centred. Script: `import { loadProduct } from '.../product-render/build.js'; const p = await loadProduct(url); const ctrl = p.mount(el, { place: 'stage', view: 'side', scene, color, mode });` The controller: `setColor(id)`, `setView(v)`, `setScene(s)`, `ready()`, `pause()`, `resume()`, `step(on)`, `set(params)`, `setPalette(p | null)`, `destroy()`. `auto.js` exports `products` (frame to controller) and `ready`. `views.html` beside this file is the worked example (every view, a scene per spec, two colour switches, one `still` mount). ## Stills and posters: run this after every change to a spec ``` node assets/objects/product-render/make-posters.mjs path/to/spec.json --profile [--port 5905] [--variants side,detail-saddle,three-quarter+loaded] [--grounds light,dark] [--px 1100] [--timeout 9] [--quiet] [--legacy] node assets/objects/product-render/make-posters.mjs --check path/to/spec.json (spec, views, scenes and shaders only) ``` It checks the spec (unknown parts, props or materials, a part a view or scene names that is not there, too many parts, shader words a laptop GPU rejects), then renders in a headless, software-rendered Chrome (its own profile, closed by its own PID, never port 3000) every variant in `spec.make.variants` (`view` or `view+scene`) on each ground in `spec.make.grounds`, and writes beside the spec: `stills/--[-dark].webp` and `-half.webp` (one still per colourway, transparent, cropped to the product and its shadow), `-.fallback-render[-dark].png` (the live render's poster) and `.stills.json` (what was made, where the product and a close-up's framed parts sit, and which sides a close-up cuts). A colourway costs no render: the accent part is lit again in each colour. Each variant is written as soon as it is made; a CPU takes one to four minutes a variant for 60-90 parts, so pass `--variants` a few at a time. `--legacy` also writes the turntable's four posters. A view with no still renders itself once on the page (`still` mode) and frees its context. ## The spec ```json { "id": "city-bike", "name": "City bicycle", "label": "A city bicycle with a front basket", "units": "m", "angle": -34, "turn": { "mode": "sway", "amp": 22, "period": 24 }, "materials": { "frame": { "kind": "paint", "color": "accent", "finish": "gloss" } }, "parts": [ { "type": "wheel", "at": [-0.53, 0.35, 0], "r": 0.35, "spokes": 36, "wall": "#c7a57a" }, { "type": "tube", "from": [-0.07, 0.29, 0], "to": [-0.23, 0.81, 0], "r": 0.017, "mat": "frame", "blend": 0.01 } ] } ``` Axes: **x forward** (the product's front), **y up**, **z across** (toward the viewer at angle 0). Any unit; the model is scaled so its largest side is one unit and set on the floor at its lowest point. Model the product from its real measurements: proportions are most of what makes it read as a render. | key | what | |---|---| | `id`, `name`, `label` | the label is what a screen reader hears ("A desk lamp, switched on") | | `poster` | the posters' file name (default the id) | | `angle` | its turn at rest and in the still, degrees (default -32: a three-quarter view) | | `turn` | `{ "mode": "sway", "amp": 26, "period": 22 }` (default), `{ "mode": "spin", "speed": 10 }`, `{ "mode": "still" }` | | `camera` | `{ "elev": 12 }` degrees above the floor | | `click` | `"light"`: a click switches every `light` material (and `glow`) on and off; it starts on | | `pool` | `{ "at": [x, 0, z], "r": 0.2 }`: the light it throws on the floor while on | | `materials` | named materials for the parts | | `motion` | moving groups (joints), below | | `colors` | colourways: `[{ "id": "blue", "name": "Deep blue", "accent": "#2c4f7c" }]` (the accent parts take it; `materials` swaps materials too, at a render each) | | `views` | close-ups and own views: `{ "detail-saddle": { "part": ["saddle*", "seat post"], "angle": -42, "elev": 16, "margin": 1.3, "cover": 2 } }` (a name ending in `*` takes every part it begins; `cover` the widest frame the shot fills, 1 for the margin alone: a close-up render of 2-3 MP takes a CPU 2-9 minutes) | | `scenes` | the product loaded or in use, below | | `supports` | the views the product draws well, `["three-quarter", "side", "front", "detail-saddle"]`: only these are offered (`product.views`), made (`make.variants` outside it fails `--check`) and mounted; list a view only after looking at its still (a bike from above reads as lying on its side, so the city bike omits `top`). Keep `three-quarter` (the default view) | | `make` | `{ "variants": ["three-quarter", "side", "detail-saddle", "three-quarter+loaded"], "grounds": ["light", "dark"], "px": 1100 }`: what make-posters makes | | `parts` | the parts, below (keep it under about 90) | ### Parts Every part takes `mat` (a material name or an inline material), `blend` (a fillet in units where it meets the parts listed before it: welded tubes, a cast body), `in` (a motion group) and `name` (for you). It is placed by `from` + `to` (a linear part runs between them; `up` turns its section), or by `at` plus `axis` (`"x"`, `"y"`, `"z"` or a vector) and/or `rot` ([x, y, z] degrees). | type | sizes | use | |---|---|---| | `tube` | `r`, `r2` (taper), `cap` `flat`/`round`, `round`, `seams` | frame tubes, posts, rods, handles, a tapered robot link | | `beam` | `w`, `d` (section), `round`, `seams` | flat bars, cranks, rails | | `box` | `size` [x, y, z], `round`, `seams` | housings, bodies, pedals, a gripper | | `panel` | `size` (thin), rounder | plates, lids, a screen's back | | `cylinder` / `disc` | `r`, `h`, `round`, `seams` | bases, hubs, motor housings, caps | | `sphere`, `ellipsoid` | `r` / `size` | a bulb, a bell, a knob | | `torus` | `R`, `r` | rings, a chainring, a status light | | `joint` | `r`, `w`, `capMat` | a hinge: knuckle about `axis` (default z) with caps on both faces | | `wheel` | `r`, `tyre` [width, height], `rim` [depth, width], `hub` [r, length], `spokes`, `spokeR`, `style` `spoked`/`disc`/`solid`, `wall` (sidewall colour), `rimMat`, `hubMat`, `spin` (deg/s) | bicycles, strollers, carts, casters; axle along `axis` (default z) | | `shade` | `from` (closed end) `to` (open end), `r1`, `r2`, `t`, `bulge` 0..1, `innerMat` | lamp shades, bells, horns, a speaker cone | | `seat` | `size` [length, height, width], `style` `saddle`/`cushion` | saddles, seats, cushions (local x forward) | | `basket` | `size`, `style` `wire`/`slats`/`solid`, `pitch`, `wire`, `rimMat` | baskets, crates, bins, trays (open top) | | `arc` | `R`, `a0`, `a1` (degrees), `r` or `size` [radial, axial] | mudguards, handles, bent frames, hoops | | `spring` | `from`, `to`, `R`, `r`, `turns` | springs, coiled cords | | `path` | `points` [[x,y,z]...], `r`, `smooth` (on with 3+ points) | handlebars, cables, bent tubes | `seams`: panel lines cut round the part at heights along its length (-1..1 of its half length): the seams of a robot's shell, a base's groove. `seamWidth`, `seamDepth` in units. ### Materials A name from `materials`, a built-in name, or `{ "kind": ..., "color": "#hex" | "accent", "finish": "gloss" | "satin" | "matte" }`. | kind | | built-in names | |---|---|---| | `paint` | enamel or powder coat; `color: "accent"` takes the page's accent | `accent`, `paint`, `white`, `black`, `graphite` | | `metal` | brushed alloy | `alloy`, `aluminium` | | `chrome` | polished | `chrome` | | `steel` | dark stainless (spokes, wire) | `steel` | | `rubber` | tyres, pads, grips | `rubber` | | `plastic` | satin plastic | `plastic` | | `wood` | oiled wood with rings; `grain` x/y/z, `scale` | `wood`, `oak`, `walnut` | | `fabric` | a fine weave; `weave` | `fabric` | | `leather` | | `leather` | | `light` | gives light; with `click: "light"` it switches | `light` | Any material takes `glow` (0..1): a lit inner face (a shade's inside when the lamp is on). ### Motion ```json "motion": [ { "id": "yaw", "pivot": [0, 0.14, 0], "axis": "y", "amp": 26, "period": 13 }, { "id": "shoulder", "parent": "yaw", "pivot": [0, 0.32, 0], "axis": "z", "amp": 9, "period": 11, "phase": 0.2 } ] ``` A group turns its parts (`"in": "shoulder"`) about `pivot` and `axis` by `rest` + `amp` x a sine of `period` seconds, after its parent. Pivots are given at rest, in the spec's units. Up to four groups. The joints move only while the product turns: a still, a phone and reduced motion show the rest pose. ### Scenes and props: the product loaded or in use ```json "scenes": { "loaded": { "label": "A city bicycle with a child seat on the rack, a crate of fruit and a pannier", "hide": ["basket"], "props": [ { "prop": "child-seat", "at": [-0.578, 0.796, 0] }, { "prop": "crate", "at": [0.6, 0.76, 0], "size": [0.3, 0.2, 0.32], "contents": "fruit" }, { "prop": "bag", "at": [-0.62, 0.42, 0.152], "hooks": true } ] }, "desk": { "lit": { "at": [0.53, 0.11], "r": 0.19, "k": 3.6 }, "pool": null, "props": [ { "prop": "desk", "at": [0.2, -0.032, 0.02] }, { "prop": "book", "at": [0.3, 0, -0.15], "count": 2 } ] } } ``` A scene adds props (and plain `parts`), hides parts by name, and may change `label`, `pool`, `click` and `materials`. `lit` throws a lamp's warm pool of light on the props' upward faces. Props are made of ordinary parts at the size of the real thing, standing on y = 0 and facing x, in metres (`scale` converts: 1000 for a spec in millimetres); each takes `at`, `yaw`, `scale`, `size`, `color`, `mats` { role: material }, `in` (a motion group: a parcel held in a gripper) and `name`. | prop | what | options | |---|---|---| | `child-seat` | a rack seat: high back, wings, cushion, shoulder and lap belts to a red buckle, footrests | `color`; roles shell, pad, belt, buckle | | `bench` | a padded bench for 1-3 children or passengers in a row (a cargo box): two belts and a buckle a seat | `seats`, `width`, `color`; roles frame, pad, belt, buckle | | `crate` | a slatted wooden crate, open on top | `size`, `contents` fruit / bottles / loaves / parcels / none | | `bag` | a pannier (flap, straps, handle, `hooks` for a rack) or `style: "tote"` | `size`, `color` | | `parcel` | a cardboard box with tape and a label | `size`, `color` | | `tray` | a low open bin with parcels standing in it | `size`, `parcels` 0-4 | | `desk` | a tabletop | `size`, `color` | | `book` | 1-3 stacked books | `count`, `colors` | | `mug` | a mug of coffee | `r`, `h`, `color` | | `sheet` | a sheet of paper | `size` | Keep a scene under about 110 parts. Its props must read at the size the page shows them (belts, buckles, a crate's slats, a bag's flap), and a scene goes where the copy promises it. ## Behaviour and limits - **It always shows a picture**: the view's still (no WebGL); without one, the poster at once and the render over it, the poster staying when WebGL fails. Under `prefers-reduced-motion`, and on a phone (max-width 700px or a coarse pointer), one still frame, drawn sharp, and the context freed. A turning product has a pause button in its frame's bottom-right corner. - **At most one live context** for a product: only the first product render mounted turns (when the page asks for the turn, or no still was made); a second holds still. The page's cap of 4 contexts (`window.__tpGl`) counts it. - **Cost**: every part is evaluated per ray step, skipped when its bounding sphere is further than the nearest part so far. About 20 parts renders like a print object; 60-70 (a bicycle with its spokes) is fine on a laptop GPU and slow on a CPU renderer (posters: about 90 s). Keep under 90. - **What it cannot do**: text or logos on the product, transparent glass, cloth that drapes, a freeform organic shell (a shoe, a face, a car body), anything thinner than about a texel (it is thickened). For those: the client's photographs or renders, never this. - **Never** a product of another kind, never on a place page, never a caption under it. The three specs in `specs/` (a city bicycle, a desk lamp, a robot arm) are worked examples, each with its views, a scene and colourways (run `make-posters.mjs` on a spec to make its stills; until then each frame renders itself once): `views.html` shows them at anchor scale with colour switches (`?only=bike|lamp|arm`, `?mode=still|live`); `demo.html` the turntable (`?turn=0`, `?fallback=1`).

objects/photo-kit/README.md:
# Photo prints A photograph printed whole by a shader in the page's ink on its own sheet: a halftone, an engraving or a dither. Hover (a tap on a phone) shows the photograph itself under the print. A print is one crafted moment on a page, never the way a page shows its photographs. | Object | Looks like | Hover | |---|---|---| | `photo-halftone` | a one-ink halftone: round dots on a 45° screen, clean paper in the light, solid ink in the deepest shadow | a loupe (round lens, hairline rim, soft shadow) shows the photograph in its own colours | | `photo-engraving` | an engraved plate: diagonal lines that swell in shadow and bend over the forms, over a light wash of the photograph's colour | the lines part around the cursor and the photograph shows through | | `photo-dither` | a three-colour grain: the photograph's deepest and most colourful colours on the paper | the photograph develops through the grain in a soft circle | Each folder's `demo.html` (served over http) shows it in the light, dark and colour palettes. `meta.json` lists its params, touch behaviour, fallback and cost. ## Where a print goes, and where not - **Yes:** one moment on a software, AI, design-tool or gaming page: the page's one photograph band, or a feature tile whose subject is the photograph (an imaging or design tool printing a picture, `tint: 1` for the brand's ink). One print per page; a row of three only on a page about prints. - **Never** over the hero photograph or a section's main photograph (`references/photos.md`): a print there reads as broken or low-resolution. Never on a café, guesthouse, shop or other local business page: those show their photographs plain. - **Never** a caption under it that explains the effect, and no note that it is a print. ## The photograph The client's own photograph first. Else one from the vetted library that prints well (one clear subject, a plain ground, clear light): ```bash node /scripts/photos.mjs list --trade office --json # entries with "prints": true node /scripts/photos.mjs fetch --out . # the files, credits.json and the ``` On a dark page pick a darker photograph (`"tone": "dark"` or `"mid"`): a pale one prints as a large light plate there. ## Mount Paste the `` that `photos.mjs fetch` prints into the frame. The print reads that picture (the largest `srcset` size), keeps its `alt`, and takes its `object-position` as the subject's place. ```html
``` - The frame needs a size (an `aspect-ratio` or a height). The print fills it, prints on the page's `--surface` so the frame reads as a sheet (`ground: 0` prints on `--bg`), and follows the page's palette (`ctrl.setPalette(fx.readPalette(el))` after a palette switch). - `focusX`/`focusY` (0..1) override the ``'s `object-position`. - The print is there from its first frame: no entry, no dissolve, nothing moves at rest. - A small UI card may sit on a corner of the frame (`cards.md`), never over the subject; never text over the print. ## Credit Credits go in the footer's one credits line, never under the print. A printed photograph counts as adapted: ```bash node /scripts/photos.mjs credits --out . --adapted ``` For a photograph that did not come through `photos.mjs`, `creditsBlock(entries, { adapted: [id] })` in `photo.js` writes the same footer block from `{ id, by, page, licence, licenceUrl, source }` (one line, "Photographs via ...", that opens the list). The client's own photograph needs none. ## When it cannot draw Before the first frame, while the canvas is released off screen, and whenever WebGL is missing, the shader fails to compile or link, or the photograph's host sends no CORS headers, the photograph itself shows, greyed into the palette: a still picture, never an empty frame. The runtime also refuses a shader that uses a GLSL ES reserved word (`flat`, `smooth`, `sample`, `filter`, `input`...) and shows the still, because a laptop's GPU rejects what CPU WebGL (SwiftShader) compiles. `glslLint(src)` and `photoShader(object)` in `photo.js` check a shader from Node. ## Cost One canvas and one WebGL context per print, paused off screen and with the tab hidden, released 1.5 s after it leaves the screen. At most 3 prints hold a context; a fourth waits (showing its still) until one leaves, and a frame scrolling away gives way to one coming in. Count them with the page's other WebGL effects (keep a page to 3 live contexts). The halftone and engraving render up to 2 canvas px per CSS px so dots and lines stay sharp; every print stays under 1.5 MP of canvas. Each pixel reads the photograph 2 to 5 times from its mipmaps; no loops.

objects/_scenes/README.md:
# Scene objects (`assets/objects/`, runtime in `_scenes`) Real things shown through a print effect, alive under the pointer. Four of them take the client's own photographs (`src`); one models a generic thing in code. Each is the picture of one card or one hero frame: still or nearly still at rest, and it moves under the pointer, never on scroll. | id | what it shows | moves by itself | hover / touch | |---|---|---|---| | `split-reveal` | one photograph, half printed as a halftone, a line between | no | the line follows the pointer; drag on touch; a slider for the keyboard | | `dither-sequence` | 2 to 6 photographs that belong together, dithered, cut one to the next | yes: holds, then wipes (pause disc) | the pointer scrubs the frames; drag on touch | | `dot-object` | one object cut out of its photograph and set in dots | no | under the pointer the dots take the photograph's real colour, like a loupe | | `exploded-layers` | one photograph (or up to four) as four printed sheets in perspective | no | the sheets open apart; with `names` each gets a label; tap on touch | | `product-turntable` | a generic camera, chair, speaker or cup on a turntable, dithered | yes: one step every 1.7 s (pause disc) | moving across turns it step by step; drag on touch | `index.json` lists them; each folder's `meta.json` has every param (and its `for` and `never`), and `demo.html` (served, not from disk) shows the object in a hero and two cards with a palette switch. ## Where they go: software pages only **A scene is a print (halftone, dither, dots) and prints belong to software, tech, AI, developer tool and games pages**, as their one moment: a hero frame or one feature card. House rule: effects fit tech or gaming sites, a local coffee shop never. - **Place, service and local-business pages** (a cafe, a bar, a shop, a hotel, a clinic, a studio people visit): no scene. Their photographs show plain, never printed as a halftone, a dither or dots (`references/photos.md`). - **Product pages** (a maker of bikes, furniture, lamps, devices): no scene. The product's own photographs show plain; without photographs its object render (`assets/objects/print-*`, `_print-core/README.md`), never a scene and never stock of something else. - **On a software page**, a scene shows a real thing the product works on or with: - `split-reveal`, `exploded-layers`: a photograph a photo, design or print tool works on, the device a tech company makes, a game's key art. `exploded-layers` labels only with `names` in the client's words (the layers its software works on); without names it opens without labels, and never names the sheets after the techniques (halftone, dither). - `dither-sequence`: two to six photographs that belong together (a device from several sides, the stages of what the software makes, a game's scenes), never a random or mood set. - `dot-object`: only an object shot on a seamless plain ground (lighter or darker than the object, or another colour), or a cut-out PNG with a clear ground. A busy or sunlit background does not cut out: use `split-reveal` instead. - `product-turntable` draws a generic thing, never the client's product: a card about a kind of thing the software handles (cameras in a rental platform's inventory, a chair in a furniture marketplace, a speaker an audio app controls). - One scene per screen, at most two on a page, and the page's other WebGL counted with them. - No caption under a scene that explains it or apologises for it ("made in code", "a print of", "a stand-in"); the card's heading and text say what the thing is. - The demo photographs are test pictures. Never ship them as the client's. ## Put one on a page ```html

Every edit on its own layer

Turn any adjustment off later without touching the rest.

``` One per object, copy and change the `src` and the words: ```html
``` - The host is an empty `div`. In a `.panel`, `.panel__screen` or `.frame` it fills the box (give the box its size: an aspect ratio or a height); elsewhere give it a size yourself. - `data-scene-src`: a page-relative path or URL, or JSON: `{ src, alt, focus: [x, y], by, page, licence, licenceUrl }`, or an array of them. Serve photographs from the site itself (a host that sends no CORS headers cannot be printed: the plain photograph shows instead). - `data-scene-params`: JSON, every param in `meta.json`. `data-scene-palette`: JSON `{ bg, ink, muted, accent }`. `aria-label`: what the picture shows (else the photograph's alt). - **Colours**: without a palette the scene prints in the page tokens (`--bg`, `--surface`, `--ink`, `--muted`, `--accent`) on the ground of the box it sits in (a `.panel` on `--surface` prints on `--surface`; a dark band prints in a light ink). It paints its own ground: put it in a plain panel, never over a dealt effect ground. - **One moving scene per group**: in a section (or a `[data-scene-group]`) only the first `product-turntable` or `dither-sequence` moves by itself, or the one with `data-scene-loop`; the others hold still until the pointer reaches them. A moving scene puts the shared 32 px pause disc (`.loop-pause`) in the box's bottom-right corner: keep that corner clear. - Text goes above or beside the panel, never over the scene. No caption that explains the effect, no chips; the photograph's credit goes in the page's one credit line. - **Credits**: `import { credits } from 'assets/objects/_scenes/kit.js'`; `credits([entry, ...])` returns the footer's one line of small print for every photograph the scenes print, each named once ("Photographs: A on Unsplash, adapted; B, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons, adapted."). Never a credit under the picture, never a line per photograph. The client's own photographs need none. - **Script**: `import obj from 'assets/objects/split-reveal/object.js'; const ctrl = obj.mount(el, { src, params, palette })`. The controller has `pause()`, `resume()`, `setPalette(p | null)`, `destroy()` and `ready` (a promise, once the photographs are in). `auto.js` exports `scenes`, a Map from element to controller; after a theme change call `setPalette(null)` on each. ## Behaviour - **Still at rest**: `split-reveal`, `dot-object` and `exploded-layers` draw once and again only while the pointer moves them. `product-turntable` and `dither-sequence` draw only while they step or wipe (30 frames a second at most) and nothing while they hold. - **Never on scroll**: nothing animates as it comes on screen; it is drawn finished. - **Reduced motion**: one still frame, no pause disc; the pointer still moves the line, the frame, the loupe and the turntable, at once. - **No WebGL, a shader that fails, or a photograph that fails**: the plain photograph (cover-cropped at its focus) takes the panel and the overlays go; the turntable shows a still of its form (`fallback-
-light|dark.png`, made by `make-fallbacks.html`). A sequence leaves a failed photograph out of the loop. The panel never stays empty: the still also goes in when a shader breaks a rule of GLSL ES 1.00 or 3.00 (`glslLint` in `kit.js` reads every shader before it is compiled), fails to compile or link, a frame throws, or the first frame comes out one flat colour. Only a photograph that cannot load at all (its host down or blocked) leaves the panel's own ground: the host gets `data-scene-empty` and the console an error. Serve the photographs from the site itself. - **Shaders**: the test Chromes render WebGL on the CPU (SwiftShader), which compiles words a laptop's GPU rejects (a struct field named `flat` once left a hero empty). After changing a shader run `node assets/objects/_scenes/lint-glsl.mjs`: it checks every scene shader as compiled and exits 1 on a reserved word, a keyword or type used as a name or field, a double underscore, an unknown `gl_` name, or a name that hides a built-in function. ## Light on a laptop GPU - Each scene has one canvas and one WebGL context, paused off screen and with the tab hidden, and freed 1.5 s after it leaves the screen; it is made again before it returns. - At most 2 scene contexts live at once (`config.live` in `kit.js`), a hard cap: off-screen ones give theirs up first, then idle ones, then still ones (each keeps its last frame as a picture). Count them with the page's grounds and other effects: keep a page to 4 live contexts. - A smooth canvas renders at most 1 canvas px per CSS px (0.75 in a frame over 1 MP for the layers) and never over 1.5 MP; a dithered one holds one canvas px per dither cell. No MSAA. Dots and layers draw from static buffers; nothing runs per frame on the CPU.

objects/_print-core/README.md:
# Objects (`assets/objects/print-*`) Everyday things modelled in 3D in code: a cup and saucer, a bicycle wheel, a desk lamp, a desk globe, playing cards. Each one is shown as a **render** (the default: a studio render in its own materials, the page's accent on one part, soft shadows and the reflections of a softbox) or as a **print** of that render (halftone, engraving, dither or type). It turns slowly, leans toward the pointer and takes one small step on a click (the lamp switches on, the cards fan out). **Where it goes** - **A product page without photographs**: the object of the product's own kind is the product's picture: the hero (`hero` preset, or `tile` in a hero split) and the statement's picture, as a render. A desk lamp for a lamp maker, a cup for a tableware maker, a wheel for a maker of wheels. Never an object of another kind: a wheel does not show a whole bicycle, a cup does not show a coffee machine. No object of its kind: compose the product itself from a spec of its parts with `../product-render` (its README), never `hero-product` without the product's picture. - **A software, tech or games page**: the one moment on a feature card or a wide frame, about the thing the card says (a globe for regions, cards for a games feature). Here a print fits. - **Not on a place page** (a cafe, a shop, a hotel, a studio people visit) and not beside the client's own photographs: those lead with photographs. - Prints (halftone, engraving, dither, type) only on software, tech, AI and games pages. A product page shows the render. - No caption under it, and no words calling it a render, a drawing, an illustration, a model, a sample or a stand-in. The section's heading and text say what the product is. Leave `aria-label` alone or name the thing plainly ("A desk lamp, switched on"). | id | the render | prints | click | |---|---|---|---| | `print-cup` | porcelain cup of coffee on its saucer, the glaze in the accent | halftone, engraving | rings run across the coffee | | `print-wheel` | road wheel: tan-wall tyre, alloy rim, 24 spokes, hub in the accent | halftone (spokes as solid lines) | it spins up | | `print-lamp` | balanced-arm desk lamp: stepped base, paired rods, chrome springs, a domed shade; base and shade enamelled in the accent | halftone | it switches on | | `print-globe` | desk globe, real coastlines, brass meridian, walnut stand | engraving | it spins | | `print-cards` | playing cards, the ace of diamonds face up, backs in the accent | halftone | the cards fan out | `index.json` lists them; each folder's `meta.json` has the object's own notes, and `demo.html` shows it full screen with switches for the picture and the paper. ## Put one on a page ```html

Regions

Pick where your data lives: 14 regions on four continents.

``` - `auto.js` mounts every `[data-print]`. The host is an empty `div`; in a `.panel`, `.panel__screen` or `.frame` it fills it and draws over the panel's ground. - **Where it sits** (`data-print-place`, or picked from the box it is in): - `card` in a `.panel`: large, cut by the bottom-left edge, as on x.ai's and Figma's feature cards; the bottom-right corner stays clear for the pause button. In a panel about as tall as wide (a card on a phone) it is cut less, so the thing still reads. The card's text sits above the panel, never over the object. - `tile` in a `.panel--top` or a square frame: whole, standing low. - `hero` in a wide `.frame`: large, right of centre, the text in the clear left half. In a frame about as tall as wide (a phone) it sits smaller and low, under the text. - `none`: centred on its own paper. - **Options**: `data-print-params='{"angle":-20}'` over the preset (every param is in `meta.json`); a print: `data-print-params='{"effect":"halftone"}'`. `data-print-palette='{"bg":..,"ink":..,"accent":..}'`. - **Colours**: on a dealt ground it draws on that ground's paper with an ink that reads on it and the page's accent; elsewhere in the page tokens (`--bg`, `--surface`, `--ink`, `--accent`). The accent goes on one part (the glaze, the hub, the shade and base, the card backs; the globe's sea when the accent is a blue or teal). Until that ground has drawn (it bakes one panel at a time, slowly on a CPU renderer, and a bake can fail), the object lays the ground's paper under itself, flat, and gives it back when the ground draws (`data-print-paper` is `own` or `ground`), so a print for dark paper never stands on a pale, undrawn panel. `blank-ground.html` tests it (`data-ready` is `pass` or `fail`). - **One loop per group**: one object per card group turns by itself (the first, or the one with `data-print-loop`); the others hold still until the pointer reaches their card. A turning object puts its own round pause button in the panel's bottom-right corner once it has drawn (never on a poster): keep that corner clear. - **Script**: `import obj from '/objects/print-cup/object.js'; const ctrl = obj.mount(el, { place: 'card', params: {...}, palette: {...} })`. The controller has `pause()`, `resume()`, `step(on)`, `set(params)`, `setPalette(p | null)`, `destroy()`. `auto.js` exports `prints`, a Map from element to controller; on a theme change call `setPalette(null)` on each. ## Do and don't - One object per card group, at most two in view, and never over a moving ground: the ground holds still (`"speed":0,"grainMotion":0`). On a product page a plain lit ground or the page's surface. - The object is the picture. No UI fragment over it, no second effect beside it. - Never centred dead in a card panel with even ground all round: use the presets. - Never animated by scroll. It moves only by its own slow turn, the pointer and a click. - The client's own photographs and screenshots come first; an object never takes their place. ## It always shows a picture - A **poster** shows at once: the object drawn ahead of time (`fallback-render.png`, or `fallback.png` for a print), in the page's palette, where the live picture will be. The live picture fades in over it. - Every shader source is checked for words a laptop's GPU rejects before it is compiled (`glslProblems` in `print3d.js`: GLSL ES reserved words, a qualifier such as `flat` used as a name, names of built-in functions, double underscores). CPU-rendered Chrome compiles some of these, so a screenshot never proves a shader builds on a real GPU. Run `node assets/objects/_print-core/lint-glsl.mjs` after changing a model (exit 1 on a problem). - A shader that fails the check, fails to compile or link, no WebGL2, a lost context, or a first frame that comes out empty: the poster stays, never an empty ground. Tests force each case with `window.__printBreak = 'compile' | 'link' | 'reserved' | 'empty'` before the object mounts, or `?fallback=1` on a demo page (no WebGL2). ## Light on a laptop GPU - All objects of a page share **2 live WebGL contexts** (`config.maxLive` in `print3d.js`), so a page with its baked grounds and one other effect stays within 3. - An object holds a context only while something on it moves near the screen (its turn, the pointer, a step). A still object draws once, keeps that frame as a plain picture and frees its context; it takes one again when the pointer comes onto its card. Off screen (beyond 40% of a screen) or in a hidden tab its context is freed. - The raymarch runs at most 1 texel per CSS pixel (0.75 x 0.75 once the frame passes about 0.48 megapixels); dither runs 1 texel per cell and its canvas holds one pixel per cell, scaled up crisp; no canvas passes about 1.5 megapixels. Slow frames lower the texels, then the march steps, then stop the turn. - A render at rest (an object that does not turn, the frame kept when its context is freed, a reduced-motion frame) is drawn once more at up to one texel per canvas pixel (`config.fineTexels`, 1.2 megatexels), so the picture that stays on the page is sharp. One frame, never a loop. - Under `prefers-reduced-motion`: one still frame, kept as a picture, and the context freed at once (none held at rest); no hover, no pause button; a click shows the step at once. ## Posters `make-fallbacks.html` makes every object's posters (open `?ids=print-cup` for one): `fallback.png` and `fallback-dark.png` are print plates (red ink, green accent, blue the silhouette); `fallback-render.png` and `fallback-render-dark.png` are twice as wide: the plates on the left (red the floor's shadow, green the accent part, blue the coverage) and the render in colour on the right, its accent part in a neutral grey that the page's accent replaces. An object whose picture depends on the palette lists extra plates (`plates`) and picks them with `poster(palette, dark, render)`: the globe has `-sea` posters for a blue accent. Make them again after every change to a model. ## A new object `definePrint({ id, name, label, press, base: import.meta.url, glsl, pivot, radius, extent, camera, turn, step, params, place, update, texture, poster, plates, posterPrint })` in `/object.js`, where `glsl` defines `vec2 map(vec3 p)` (distance, material id; y up, the floor at y = 0) and `void surf(float id, vec3 p, vec3 n, inout Surf s)`, which sets the print's tone (`albedo`, `gloss`, `wire`, `lo`, `hi`) and, when `u_render > 0.5`, the render's material (`col` in linear colour, `metal`, `gloss`, `shine`, `accent`). The header of `print3d.js` lists the rest. Model it as the real thing (proportions, parts, materials) so the render reads as a product shot, not a drawing; run the lint, make its posters, and check it at 1440, 820 and 390 on light and dark paper. If it still looks cheap after two honest tries, drop it.

moments/gallery.html:
Moments

13 creative moments, one or two a page on every kind; a place, product or service page is dealt only the photo- and type-led ones that list it (references/moments.md). Each link is a full demo page; the moment is marked data-moment in its source.

  • Counter rolls text · statement · enter · tech, gaming, software

    The digits of two to four proof figures roll once like an odometer when the row comes on screen, the right-most digit turning most; the strips rest on the real figures before and after, so the row never reads as zeros.

    Phone and reduced motion: The figures stand.

  • Cursor spotlight hover · hero · pointer · tech, gaming, software

    A soft light on the hero's ground follows the pointer with a short lag and shows a fine dot grid around it; it drifts back to its resting spot when the pointer leaves.

    Phone and reduced motion: The light rests at its spot; there is no pointer.

  • Giant type, picture passing scroll · statement · scroll · tech, gaming, software

    Two to four words set at 12vw with a photograph showing through the letters under a 35% ink tint; the photograph passes upward through the type as the section crosses the screen.

    Phone and reduced motion: The photograph stands still in the letters, the type smaller (19vw).

  • Iris opens transition · section · scroll · tech, gaming, software

    A section that sits on a new ground keeps that ground edge to edge; inside it an inset panel in the old ground (even gutter, card corners, never touching the section's edges) opens a disc in the middle of what is visible, widening with a hairline accent ring at its edge. Each heading, paragraph, button and picture stays hidden until the disc holds all of it, then fades in whole, so no word is ever cut.

    Phone and reduced motion: The section stands on its own ground, no panel, no ring.

  • Letters assemble scroll · statement · scroll · tech, gaming, software

    A statement of two to five words, set very large: its letters start scattered, shifted and turned, and fly into the line one after the other as the statement rises through the screen, whole before it reaches the middle.

    Phone and reduced motion: The statement stands as written, in a smaller size.

  • Line carries the colour transition · section · scroll · tech, gaming, software

    A section that sits on a new ground keeps that ground edge to edge; inside it an inset panel in the old ground (even gutter, card corners, never touching the section's edges) is cleared by a one-pixel accent line that climbs through it from its foot to its top: below the line the section's own ground and words, above it the old ground. Each heading, paragraph, button and picture stays hidden until the line has passed above all of it, then fades in whole, so no word is ever cut.

    Phone and reduced motion: The section stands on its own ground, no panel, no line.

  • Liquid hover liquid · hero, section · hover · WebGL · tech, gaming, software

    The pointer pushes a photograph like the surface of water: the picture bends along the pointer's path with a wet shine and a hair of colour split, and the ripple diffuses away in a second or two, back to the plain picture.

    Phone and reduced motion: The plain photograph, no canvas, no WebGL context.

  • Liquid type liquid · hero, statement · pointer · tech, gaming, software

    A very large headline ripples and stretches like type seen through water wherever the pointer crosses it, and settles back to crisp type within about a second; one SVG filter, only while it moves.

    Phone and reduced motion: The headline stands as written; there is no pointer.

  • Marquee row scroll · section · loop · tech, gaming, software

    One row of client words, trades, cities or formats moves slowly sideways in a loop, fading at both edges; it pauses under the pointer and has a pause button.

    Phone and reduced motion: The words stand in a wrapped row; nothing runs.

  • Photo chapters scroll · section · scroll · place, product, service

    A short story in three to five photographs, one large frame at a time: the section holds on screen while, under its h2, one photograph the width of the page is uncovered by the next from its foot upward, settling from a slight zoom, and a panel in the page's ground on the photograph's lower left changes to that chapter (its number, a title and two lines). Each chapter has about two thirds of a screen of scroll: the wipe takes under half of it and the photograph holds for the rest. Live at every width on a screen 600px or taller, phones included.

    Phone and reduced motion: It runs on a phone held upright (one photograph at a time, the panel across its foot); a phone turned sideways, under 600px tall, gets the chapters stacked, each photograph over its words.

  • Picture develops transition · section, hero · enter · place, product, service

    One large photograph develops once as it comes on screen. On a place, product or service page (look "film") it comes up out of the paper like a print in the developer tray: a faint grey print at first, its darks arriving before its light tones, then its colour, while it settles from a slight zoom, about 1.6 s. The halftone look ("print", a two-tone dot print in the page's ground and ink giving way to the photograph) is not dealt: tech leaves this moment out, so it is kept only as opts look "print".

    Phone and reduced motion: The film look runs on a phone too (one picture, a filter and a transform, once); the print look shows the photograph.

  • Pinned chapters scroll · section · scroll · tech, gaming, software, product, service

    A feature section holds on screen for two screens of scroll while its three steps open one at a time at the left and one frame at the right changes to each step's picture with a short crossfade.

Questions before you book

How fit do I need to be?

You ride 30 to 62 km a day at a conversational pace, with one climb on day one. Anyone who rides a few hours a week will be fine.

Can I bring my own bike?

Yes. The van carries bags only, so the bike rides every day. We also hire road and gravel bikes for €45 a day.

What if the weather turns?

We ride in rain. In a storm the day's stage goes by van and the guesthouse keeps the room.

How do I get to the start?

The ride starts at the station in Bergen at 10:00 on the first day and ends at a station on the same line.

effects/README.md:
# Effects 25 effect grounds drawn in code, for hero frames, feature cards and bands. Each one takes all its colours from the page palette. Nothing here loads a video or another library; only the photo grade takes an image, the section's own photograph. - `gallery.html` shows every effect live, with a palette switcher, a random pick and the UI kit's feature cards. `lab.html` has a slider for every param and card, wide and hero layouts. - Both pages need http, not `file://`. Run `node scripts/effects.mjs serve --port 5230` and open `/assets/effects/gallery.html`. ## Mount Give an element a size and a `data-fx` id, then mount every one on the page: ```html
``` - **Palette.** Each element reads `--bg`, `--surface`, `--ink`, `--muted`, `--accent` and `--accent-ink`, or `--fx-bg` and the other `--fx-*` names, which win. You can also pass one: `fx.mountAll(document, { bg, surface, ink, muted, accent, accentInk })`. To change a single colour on one element, use `data-fx-palette='{"accent":"#..."}'`. - **Seed.** `data-fx-seed` fixes the composition. Without a seed you get a new picture on every load. - **Params.** `data-fx-params='{"speed":0.3}'`. `index.json` lists each param with its range. Text on an effect: set `calmX` and `calmY` (0 to 1 of the frame) to where the text sits. The effect keeps that area quiet. - **One element.** `const c = await fx.mount(el, 'caustics', { palette, seed, params })`. The result `c` has `pause()`, `resume()`, `set(params)`, `setPalette(p)` and `destroy()`. - **Built in.** An effect stops drawing when it leaves the screen or the tab is hidden. Under `prefers-reduced-motion` it shows one still frame. Without WebGL it shows a CSS picture in the same colours. Device pixel ratio is capped (1.75 unless an effect needs crisp pixels). When a page has more than 14 live WebGL contexts, the idle off-screen ones are freed first. - Put text and UI fragments inside the element. The canvas sits under them (`z-index: -1` in an isolated element). ## Random pick A page gets its effects dealt, never chosen by taste. One effect per slot: `hero` is the hero or a large split frame, `card` is a card group, `band` is a wide band or the closing call to action, and `footer` is the footer. Only effects made for the page's palette kind (`palettes` in meta.json) and that slot are dealt, never the same id twice on one page (when every effect for a slot is on the page already, one repeats with its own seed and pick prints a note). The command needs `--palette`; in the browser, a call without a palette deals only effects made for all three kinds. Ids from recent pages and second picks from a family already dealt are less likely. Two effects that list each other in `avoidWith` never share a page. A **focal** ground (`"focal": true`) has its own subject: a sphere, a beam, peaks, a pool of light. It takes one compact UI piece, never a big window, a screenshot or text. `--quiet` (`quiet: true` in the browser) deals only the even, **quiet** grounds, for a slot that carries a big window. Four effects are never dealt (`"random": false` in meta.json): `dotted-globe` (a literal subject, only for a product whose reach is global: payments, infrastructure, logistics, networks), `duotone-grade` (grades the section's own photograph), `edge-glow` (the lit border of the one key object, a prompt box or the featured plan) and `ridgeline` (the divider band in `assets/components/fx-band`). Name one in its slot when the content calls for it. It is still refused on a palette kind or a slot it is not made for, when the same id is named twice, and next to an effect it avoids (named or passed in `--exclude`): ```bash node scripts/effects.mjs pick --palette dark --slots hero,card,band --seed 4821 --history .taste-skill/effects-history.json node scripts/effects.mjs pick --palette dark --slots hero:dotted-globe,card,band --seed 4821 --history .taste-skill/effects-history.json ``` In the browser, the same code: ```js import { pick } from './assets/effects/pick.js'; const index = await fetch('./assets/effects/index.json').then(r => r.json()); const { picks } = pick(index.effects, { palette: fx.paletteKind(palette), slots: ['hero', 'card', 'card'], history }); // picks: [{ slot: 'hero', id: 'god-rays' }, ...]; history: the ids of earlier picks, oldest first // a named slot: slots: ['hero:dotted-globe', 'card'] (or { slot: 'hero', id: 'dotted-globe' }) ``` `fx.paletteKind(palette)` gives `light`, `dark` or `colour` from the background colour. ## The list | id | Name | Family | Slots | Palettes | Ground | Motion | |---|---|---|---|---|---|---| | `film-light-leak` | Film light leak | Grain | hero, card, band | dark, colour | focal | slow | | `grain-gradient` | Grain gradient | Grain | hero, card, band, footer | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `ascii-shade` | ASCII shade | Dither | hero, card, footer | light, dark, colour | focal | slow | | `bayer-dither` | Bayer dither | Dither | hero, card, band, footer | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `halftone-screen` | Halftone screen | Dither | hero, band | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `line-engraving` | Line engraving | Dither | hero, card, band | light, dark, colour | quiet | still | | `aurora-curtains` | Aurora curtains | Mesh | hero, band, footer | dark, colour | focal | slow | | `gradient-mesh` | Gradient mesh | Mesh | hero, card, band | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `painterly-landscape` | Painterly landscape | Mesh | hero, card | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `god-rays` | God rays | Light | hero, band | dark, colour | focal | slow | | `orb-sphere` | Light orb | Light | hero, card, band | light, dark, colour | focal | slow | | `prism-dispersion` | Prism light | Light | hero, card, band | dark | focal | slow | | `soft-light-bars` | Soft light bars | Light | hero, card, band, footer | light, dark, colour | focal | slow | | `spotlight-cone` | Stage spotlight | Light | hero, card | dark, colour | focal | slow | | `caustics` | Water caustics | Light | hero, card, band | light, dark, colour | focal | slow | | `edge-glow` | Edge glow (named only) | Light | card | light, dark, colour | border | slow | | `dot-terrain` | Dot terrain | Pattern | hero, card, band | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `grid-pulse` | Grid pulse | Pattern | hero, card, band | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `ruled-grounds` | Ruled dot ground | Pattern | card, band | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `contour-lines` | Topographic contours | Pattern | hero, card, band, footer | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `dotted-globe` | Dotted globe (named only) | Pattern | hero, card, band | light, dark, colour | focal | slow | | `ridgeline` | Ridgeline (named only) | Pattern | band | light, dark, colour | focal | slow | | `fluted-glass` | Fluted glass | Material | hero, card, band | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `silk-folds` | Silk folds | Material | hero, card, band | light, dark, colour | quiet | slow | | `duotone-grade` | Duotone grade (named only) | Photo | hero, card, band | light, dark, colour | quiet | still | Each effect's one-line description is the `look` field in `index.json`. `node scripts/effects.mjs list` prints this table, and you can filter it with `--family`, `--on`, `--palette`, `--motion` and `--quiet`. A filter value that does not exist is an error, not an empty list. Retired on 31 Oct because they looked bad or cheap: `riso-print`, `ink-bloom`, `liquid-chrome`, `metaballs`, `brushed-metal` and `paper-texture`, then `terrazzo-speckle` (a kitchen floor), `marble-warp` (zebra stripes), `pixel-mosaic` (broken JPEG blocks), `truchet-arcs` (thick grey worms) and `soft-particles` (stock bokeh). They are not in the index. `ridgeline` reads as a record cover when dealt on its own, so it is named only. ## Commands ```bash node scripts/effects.mjs index # rebuild index.json from every /meta.json and effect.js node scripts/effects.mjs gallery # write gallery.html and lab.html from scripts/*.template.html node scripts/effects.mjs publish # the gallery as one folder: publish/index.html, effects/, ui/, files.json ``` Edit the templates in `scripts/`, not `gallery.html` or `lab.html`. `publish` rebuilds both pages, then copies only the files the gallery loads. `files.json` lists them, all at relative paths. ## Adding an effect A folder `/` with two files: - `meta.json`: `id`, `name`, `family` (grain, dither, mesh, light, pattern, material or photo), `look` (one sentence), `bestOn`, `palettes`, `motion` (`still`, `slow` or `interactive`) and `cost`. Optional: `"random": false` for a literal subject that is only named, never dealt; `"focal": true` for a ground with its own subject; `avoidWith` (ids that never share its page); `subjects` (what a named effect is for). - `effect.js`: `export default { id, name, family, params, mount(el, { palette, params, seed }) }`. `mount` returns `{ destroy, pause, resume }`. - For a fragment shader, use `fx.shader(el, { frag, schema, params, palette, seed, fallback })`. It handles the canvas, the lifecycle, the DPR cap, the context budget and the CSS fallback. - For canvas 2D, use `fx.lifecycle(el, { draw })`. - An effect that makes its own WebGL context calls `fx.glBudget(holder)` just before, so the context counts in the page's budget (see `dotted-globe`). Every colour comes from the palette, mixed in OKLab (`fx.color`). Never use a fixed hue, and never default to violet or lavender. Text on an effect must read at 4.5:1. Keep shader code small enough to compile fast: the D3D compiler behind Chrome on Windows inlines every function call. A helper called 16 times took 40 s to compile. Loops counted by a uniform avoid that (see `halftone-screen`). Run `index`, then check the effect in the gallery in light, dark and colour.
effects/gallery.html:
Effects library

Effects for hero frames and feature cards

Grain, dither, mesh, light, liquid, pattern and material grounds, drawn in code. Every colour comes from the page palette, and each page is dealt its own at random.

Hero

All effects

Each one live, in the palette above. A tile names the effect, its family and the slots it is made for.

On feature cards

Four effects dealt for card slots, each under a fragment from the UI kit. Random pick deals a new set.

Ask in plain words

Ask about any project or document. Every answer links to its source.

Ground:

Hand off busy work

Show it a task once. It repeats the steps for you and asks before it publishes.

Ground:

See what changed

A short weekly report shows what went up, what went down and why.

Ground:

Connect your tools

Slack, Notion, Figma and GitHub connect in a few clicks.

Ground:

Every effect is drawn in code: no images, no video. It pauses when it leaves the screen, holds one still frame under reduced motion and falls back to a CSS picture without WebGL.

Parameters and layouts

components/index.html:
Effect components
Effects library

Effects as parts of the page, not only behind it

Feature cards, real objects drawn in dither, type, numbers, buttons, borders, icons, a street map of the real place, a globe, charts and a photograph in its own colours. Every part takes its colours from the page palette: switch it at the top right. Parts that loop have a pause button.

Each component is a folder in assets/components with its markup, CSS, script and a meta.json that says what it is for and which effects suit it. Use one strong effect moment per page; the rest stay quiet. _lab.html?c=fx-chart&fx=ruled-grounds&palette=white-link-blue shows one part with another effect.

Brand marks from Simple Icons. Meeting room photograph by Breather (Unsplash licence), from the skill's photo kit. Map data © OpenStreetMap contributors.

components/fx-map/meta.json:
{
  "id": "fx-map",
  "name": "Street map of the place",
  "for": "A contact or visit section: the real streets, water, parks and rails around the place from OpenStreetMap, drawn in the page's colours, with the pin, a scale bar and an address card with working actions. No map service at run time, no key, no tracking.",
  "effects": [
    "contour-lines",
    "ruled-grounds",
    "dot-terrain"
  ],
  "default": "none",
  "how": "Bake the place once: node assets/components/fx-map/bake.mjs --lat <lat> --lon <lon> --out map.json (one request to an Overpass server; no walk by default: --from auto or --from lat,lon --from-name \"Name\" draws a walk only when the brief names a station). Paste the JSON inline as <script type=\"application/json\" class=\"cx-map__data\">...</script> inside the section, or name the file with data-cx-map. With a walk, the bake prints it in minutes and the station: write the same in the card and in the svg's aria-label. The card gives the street and district only, never a house number, postcode or coordinates. The part fits the pin, the walk and both names into the free part of the frame (right of the card from 900px of width, the whole map below it), sets street names only where they fit, and keeps every mark inside the frame. Light pages get white streets on a land a step darker than the page, dark pages lighter streets on a land a step lighter; water and parks keep a natural blue and green mixed into the land. The effects listed are only the fallback when there is no baked data (the bake could not reach the network): report it.",
  "rules": [
    "The pin is the real place: the bake's lat and lon are the address, and the address is a real street near it.",
    "Get directions opens a search for the street and district in a real map service (openstreetmap.org/search?query=Street%20District), in a new tab: never coordinates and never a route.",
    "The OpenStreetMap credit (ODbL) goes in the page's one footer credit line, never on the map and never as a caption.",
    "Nothing moves at rest. Pointed at (or its directions link focused), the walk is drawn from the station to the door and the halo answers once; nothing on scroll, so no pause button.",
    "An address the client has not given yet is a placeholder listed in the report, never a 'sample' tag on the card."
  ],
  "a11y": "A labelled region with a real address element and buttons; the svg has role img and an aria-label that names the place, the street and the walk. The pin, names and walk chip are decorative. Copy address announces by its own label change. Reduced motion: no drawn walk, no halo."
}

Each is a small signed-distance model in its own shader, mounted with fx.shader (lazy WebGL context, paused off screen and in a hidden tab). The shader runs once per dither cell, not per pixel: the canvas has one pixel per 3 CSS px cell (2 px on a stage under 420px) on every screen and is scaled up pixelated, rays that miss the object skip the march, and it draws 20 frames a second. Under reduced motion it is drawn once and kept as a picture (still: no context). The accent paints one part (the ear cups, the seat and back, the camera's body band, the drone's shell), its shaded side in a deep accent. The stage is the card tone with a 4:3 aspect; a pause button sits in its top-right corner. The print is the render to use. data-cx-render=\"studio\" (a smooth shaded render of the same form) exists but is not for pages yet: at one sample per CSS pixel its edges stair-step and the forms read as toys next to a real product shot.     const id = q.get('palette') || 'white-link-blue';
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(PALETTES[id] || PALETTES['white-link-blue'])) root.style.setProperty('--p-' + k, v);
    root.dataset.ground = q.get('ground') || 'sand';
    if (q.get('radius')) root.dataset.radius = q.get('radius');
    if (q.get('tone')) root.style.setProperty('--tone', '#' + q.get('tone'));          // e.g. ?tone=c8f2e6&toneink=0f2d27: a second brand tone
    if (q.get('toneink')) root.style.setProperty('--tone-ink', '#' + q.get('toneink'));
    root.dataset.palette = id;
    addEventListener('DOMContentLoaded', () => {
      if (q.get('bar') === '0') document.body.classList.add('no-bar');
      if (q.get('labels') === '0') document.body.classList.add('no-labels');
      const only = q.get('only');
      if (only) { const list = only.split(','); const main = document.querySelector('main'); main.style.display = 'flex'; main.style.flexDirection = 'column'; document.querySelectorAll('[data-g]').forEach(el => { const i = list.indexOf(el.dataset.g); if (i < 0) el.hidden = true; else el.style.order = i; }); }
      const bar = document.querySelector('.demo-bar');
      if (bar) {
        const sel = bar.querySelector('select[name=palette]');
        Object.keys(PALETTES).forEach(k => sel.add(new Option(k, k, false, k === id)));
        const gsel = bar.querySelector('select[name=ground]');
        gsel.value = root.dataset.ground;
        bar.addEventListener('change', () => { const u = new URL(location); u.searchParams.set('palette', sel.value); u.searchParams.set('ground', gsel.value); location = u; });
      }
    });
  })();
